InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors

Nov 27, 2026 21 min read

A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.

Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.

However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.

Microsoft Ignite 2026; Explore What's Next in AI and Software Engineering - Learn how to architect agentic systems, modernize cloud infrastructure, and tackle emerging engineering challenges. Get practical insights from Microsoft experts and industry leaders. Watch on demand.

In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.

Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.

I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.

This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.

For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.

For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.

For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.

For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.

The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.

I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.

This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.

I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.

A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.

Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author)

Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.

A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.

Why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.

For example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.

Sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.

The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.

Measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.

A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes quickly.

The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.

Interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.

When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.

A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.

A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.

A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.

Normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.

The system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.

At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.

Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.

These checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.

These are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.

Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.

This does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.

Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.

The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.

The final stage produces more than an event label.

A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.

This information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.

It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?"

These six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.

The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.

This is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.

The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.

Imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.

One morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.

The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.

The engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.

The discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.

The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.

Figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author)

The team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.

The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.

The team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.

This approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.

The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.

The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.

Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.

An accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.

The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.

A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.

The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.

Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.

A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.

The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.

The sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.

This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when users reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.

Figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author)

The team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.

The detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.

When orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.

The team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.

This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.

The lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.

The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.

The quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.

The preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.

I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.

This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.

Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.

The route display may tolerate a less frequent location update. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.

Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.

Instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.

This approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.

Engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.

Abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.

The system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.

This is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.

A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.

I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.

These measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.

I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a new application version altered sampling behavior.

This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.

A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.

The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.

On the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.

The system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.

These concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.

I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.

The goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.

A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.

The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.

The six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.

Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.

Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.

Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.

The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.

The phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.

The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

#9856. Pimalaya goes stable

Himalaya v3, Neverest, Cardamum, Calendula and Carillon v1, Ortie and Comodoro v3, all at the top of the first stable version of pimdir. Why everything at once, how it was done, where the wizard went, and what comes next.

It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard. Here the list:

Most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody. This post explains why, how, and where it goes from here. It is long, feel free to jump to the tool you care about.

In Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk. This release is the result of both.

The thing is, every piece is now connected:

Releasing them one by one meant releasing tools that disagree with each other: one version of the store here, another version of the output there. So I decided to bring every tool to release level first, then to release them all together. It took way longer than I wanted, but this way what you install today is one coherent family.

The other reason is the contract. The CLIs are not only used by humans anymore: they are used by scripts, by frontends (the Vim plugin, the TUI, the Android app), and by AI agents through MCP. All of them need a stable, versioned contract: the same JSON shapes, the same error codes, the same exit codes. Majors are the right moment to fix it, and from now on it should not move anymore without a new major.

Specs before code. Every repository has a cairn/ folder holding its living spec, its change proposals and a dated log. Every behaviour change goes through a proposal, then gets folded into the spec. This way the truth is written somewhere, and not only in my head.

One shared kit. The pimalaya-cli and pimalaya-config libs hold everything the CLIs have in common: the output contract, the error codes, the REPL, the MCP server, the configuration loading. In fact most of the work of this release was moving code from the CLIs into this kit, and deleting the copies.

One unified API, as a union. Before, the commands shared by every backend were the intersection of what the backends could do: if one backend could not do it, nobody could. Now it is the union: each backend registers the capabilities it really serves, with the same observable result as the others, and a command an account cannot serve fails before even connecting, with a clear capability-missing code.

Measured gates for pimdir. Audits always find something, so "no new finding" never ends. Instead, I built a test generator that produces stores, remote states and an oracle from a seed, and ran campaigns of 4,180 jobs against io-pimdir: crashes injected at every step, the search index checked against a full rebuild after each event, the sync engine replayed against scripted servers. The rule was simple: 2 campaigns in a row without any spec break, then freeze. Campaign 1 found one, campaigns 2 and 3 were clean, a late fix restarted the count, then campaigns 4 and 5 were clean. Freeze.

Live tests on real providers. Every CLI was tested against real accounts: Google, Microsoft, Fastmail and iCloud, plus few Chinese providers for Himalaya (QQ, 163, 139). A last "live night" just before the release found few bugs that went straight into the libs.

Libs first, apps after. The libs were released between the 13th and the 25th of November, the apps then moved to them without any patch or git pin. Everything you install comes from crates.io.

pimdir is a local-first standard for personal information: mails, contacts, calendars, tasks and files in one portable store, kept as a replica of every source, and searchable with one query language. A store is one SQLite file plus a content-addressed blob directory, the same on every OS and architecture. I already explained why such a standard is needed in Another year with NLnet, and how the Android app became its first full implementation in Pimalaya for Android enters closed alpha.

It comes in 3 parts, versioned separately:

They are released together because a store holds sync state that follows the sync part, and the query language binds every program that offers search.

What v1 means: schema version 1 never changes, every schema change is a migration, and a minor version only adds test cases. You can implement it in any language that speaks SQLite, use the I/O-free core of io-pimdir (like the Android app does, on the platform SQLite), or use its std client.

Few days before the freeze, I compared it with notmuch, which is the reference in this area. They do not do the same job (notmuch indexes mail files it does not own, pimdir owns the bodies, syncs them and holds other domains), but the search can be compared. On a store of 1 million messages from the Enron corpus, pimdir was ahead of notmuch on 50 of the 51 query measures and tied the last one, imported the million faster, and used a third of the memory. Stemming, regex and per-thread queries are still missing, they are on the list.

One warning for the early adopters: a store written by a draft version is refused, never migrated. Sync it till nothing is pending with the last draft binary, move its directory aside, then let a release create and sync a new one.

This is the change many of you will not like, so let me explain it properly.

Every CLI had a configuration wizard: you typed your email address, it discovered the servers, asked for the password, stored it in your keyring, and wrote the TOML for you. It is gone, from every CLI.

The direction. The CLIs are now low-level tools: plain text to glance at, JSON for scripts, frontends and agents. Comfort (tables, colours, relative dates, guided setups, rich composition) belongs to frontends. In fact this is not new: it is the same split that started the whole project, back when the logic left the Vim plugin. The CLI was always supposed to be the backend a frontend needs. This release just goes all the way.

I know some of you used the wizard to get started, and that copying a sample feels like a step back. If the welcome or the samples are not clear enough, it is a bug: please open an issue, I would rather fix the docs than bring back a second setup system per CLI.

Himalaya is now a low-level CLI over a unified mail API: the same commands on every backend, the protocol-specific ones next to them, plain text for a glance and --json for the rest.

Backends: IMAP, SMTP, ManageSieve, JMAP, the Gmail API, Microsoft Graph, Maildir (with a new maildir++ layout for Dovecot and Courier stores), mbox, and pimdir. The README has recipes for Proton Mail (through Bridge), Fastmail, Gmail, Outlook, Posteo and iCloud.

What is gone: the wizard, the m2dir backend (superseded by pimdir), the table and colour options, HIMALAYA_CONFIG. Unknown configuration keys are now refused, JSON keys are camelCase, and the v2 search syntax needs to be rewritten. The migration guide lists everything, with a full table for the queries.

Neverest is rebuilt around the pimdir store: every account syncs into one shared store, which the other CLIs read, search and queue their writes into. It syncs mails, contacts and calendars over IMAP, Gmail, Microsoft Graph, Google Calendar, Google People, CalDAV and CardDAV.

JMAP sources are not supported yet (it is a draft), so Fastmail syncs over IMAP, CardDAV and CalDAV for now. Coming from v0.x? Your configuration and state are not carried over: start from the config.sample.toml, then run neverest sync --init.

The first stable release of Cardamum: a low-level CLI over a unified contacts API, with the same commands on CardDAV, JMAP, Microsoft Graph, Google People, vdir and pimdir.

card search speaks the pimdir query language on every backend, account capability shows what an account serves without connecting, and you get the REPL and the MCP server like the others. Editing a card is left to a composer such as tcard. The wizard and the discover route are gone.

Same story for calendars: the same commands on CalDAV, JMAP (new), Google Calendar, Microsoft Graph, vdir and pimdir.

New: event search, recurrence expansion, attendees and alarms, online meetings (--online-meeting), invitation replies through pimdir, and an agenda that draws a month or a year like cal(1) does. Editing an event is left to a composer such as tcal. The wizard, the tables and colours, and the todo and journal commands are gone: tasks and journals will move to dedicated tools (Unfog and Journal), not released yet.

Carillon is a local watcher that fires hooks on what changes in your mailboxes, address books and calendars, over IMAP, JMAP, Maildir, CalDAV, CardDAV, Microsoft Graph, the Google APIs and the pimdir store. It uses push where the server offers it (IMAP IDLE, the JMAP event stream) and polls elsewhere. A hook runs a command, shows a desktop notification, or both.

New in v1: a pimdir backend, on-alarm-trigger for the alarms of events and tasks, on-birthday-trigger for birthdays and anniversaries, a per-hook timeout, and a report of what moved while an IMAP or Gmail session was lost. Hooks now take the same shape as Comodoro's.

Ortie manages OAuth tokens for the other tools. v3 aligns it on the rest of the family: ready-made Google, Microsoft and Fastmail accounts to paste, token revocation, an auth listen to catch a redirection handed off from another machine, account checks, a REPL, and an MCP server that never hands the token to the agent. The wizard and the hooks are gone (the storage write command does what a hook did).

Comodoro manages timers: one server owns a timer, any number of clients drive it, over a local socket or TCP. v3 joins the same standard: comodoro watch feeds a status bar without polling, hooks get the cycle name and duration, plus the welcome, account checks, a REPL and an MCP server. Comodoro is now a binary only: the library is gone, and the open JSON-RPC protocol is the contract for third parties.

None of the above would exist without the libs below, all released in November on crates.io:

They are all I/O-free, as usual: feel free to build your own tools at the top of them.

Each README lists the ways to install: prebuilt binaries from the GitHub releases (or the install.sh script), cargo install --locked, Nix, and the APT, DNF and Homebrew repositories at pkg.pimalaya.org. The packages are landing there over the coming days, and the nixpkgs and home-manager updates are on their way.

Special thanks to the NLnet foundation and the European Commission's NGI initiative, for the financial support through NGI Zero Core and now the NGI Zero Commons Fund. This kind of slow, deep work is only possible thanks to them.

And thank you to everyone who reported bugs, tested betas, or simply waited patiently while everything was being rebuilt. Any feedback is welcomed, on GitHub, on Matrix or on Mastodon. Let me know how it goes!

#9855. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#9854. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month it was PHP2Shell. This week it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discussthe PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical and operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: That's actually the one thing that occurred to me, when Web people were like, we need to take the site down while we figure things out. And I was like, just a couple of weeks prior, we had people taking down their Citrix boxes because there was a vulnerability and we didn't know what was going on. We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. Because I'm worried that we're kind of moving into this state of turning it off every time, and that's just not practical.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

Are you willing to take that risk? Are you going to be held responsible for taking that risk? And who's going to be the C-suite person or the operational leader whoever makes that call that's going to say, "Yeah, go ahead and pull the plug"?

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. Because if I'm a CISO, I wouldn't want to be making that decision about shutting down a hospital or a nuclear power plant. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. One was with an analyst who said the CISO's job is and has always been to manage risk to the best of their ability and then take the blame when things go wrong. And she was very clear that that has not changed in the age of AI; it is the continuation of a pattern.

You know, debatable, but on some days I'm sure that feels true if you're a CISO. Another conversation I had recently was about CISO risk and the need for … I think there's some growing murmurs in the CISO community about the need to push back on the risk that is not actually security's bag to hold and be a little bit more vocal and clear about offloading some of that risk to people who are really better equipped and paid to hold it.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

You can't have a team on standby 24/7 all the time responding to every alarm that goes off. It's not cost-effective. It's unrealistic. But to be fair, you have to be prepared to respond to that in some way.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

I think I saw it on a tea towel somewhere, but stay calm and look for signs. I think that's what I'm trying to do. I don't really have a good handle on where this is going next. I don't know that anybody does. So, it seems like that's the best that any security team can do. You know, focus on risk, focus on potential impact and prioritizing actions based on that. And in the meantime, to Dave's point, we'll try to avoid communal hysteria and do what we can do when we can do it, as fast as we can do it, and as smartly as we can do it. And I think that's all anybody can ask because, you know, we've never been here before.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. Know what you're securing, keep an eye on how you're working, you know, keeping an eye on your alerts. Yes, everything is a little new because we're now kind of in this age of, you know, things are being found more complicated, faster, but it's still the fundamentals, right? We need to know what we have so that we can secure it quickly and efficiently communicate it. To Dave's point, let's hope that we don't have these kinds of disastrous months every single month because I don't think we're going to be able to keep up with that volume

So, I'm going to say thank you so much for joining me for this month's Reporters' Notebook. I hope you enjoyed the conversation as much as I did. And see you next month.

Fahmida Y. Rashid is an award-winning B2B cybersecurity journalist with over two decades of experience covering enterprise technology. As editor-in-chief, she leads Dark Reading's editorial strategy. #9852. Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

November's monthly security release patches seven critical PHP flaws that should be addressed ASAP, though experts say exploitability varies and depends heavily on configuration.

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, according to PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of threat actors targeting PHP2Shell — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, the rush to patch created a fervor across the security industry hardly seen since Log4Shell in 2021.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through the project's downloads page, in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in the changelog, the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw CVE-2026-115560; use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw CVE-2026-129182; time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-129496; use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug CVE-2026-129481; use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug CVE-2026-129474; PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug CVE-2026-129289; and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-126714.

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published an analysis of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the product2shell monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9850. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9849. [$] Tainting (or not) on manual driver binding

Early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.
