#9781. Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 23: Cyber insurers share their view of the AI-driven threat landscape and how mounting challenges are putting pressure on both sides of the policy, leaving the current model unsustainable.

Cyber insurance providers are approaching 2027 facing a fundamental challenge. Claims rose 40% in 2024 and another 20% in 2025, even as premiums have stayed largely flat. This trend is something both Coalition and Travelers say isn't sustainable; and at the center of that shift is AI, which is reshaping the threat landscape not by inventing new attack types, but by making existing ones — ransomware, business email compromise, and phishing — dramatically easier to execute at scale.

In this episode of Dark Reading Confidential, Dark Reading media and projects director Becky Bracken and Dark Reading senior news director Rob Wright sit down with Lauren Winchester, vice president of cyber-risk services at Travelers; and Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition, to unpack what the data actually shows. The conversation moves past the headline-grabbing surge in disclosed vulnerabilities to a more nuanced picture: exploitation is rising, but not as sharply as disclosure volume, while AI-powered phishing kits are bring sold SaaS-style to criminals with little technical skill, driving a measurable spike in BEC and ransomware activity.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

The two insurers also agree on where the real exposure lies: not necessarily with large enterprises, which have the resources to track threat intelligence and patch quickly, but with small and mid-sized businesses that often lack an in-house IT team altogether. That awareness gap, they argue, is where insurers now have to step in — not just to underwrite risk, but to actively help policyholders defend their organizations against it.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please listen to the podcast or watch the video.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Dark Reading Confidential, a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, where we bring you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. My name is Becky Bracken. I'm an editor with Dark Reading, and I am thrilled today to do just that: deliver as promised, along with my colleague Rob Wright. Today we are going to be talking about all things cyber insurance and AI. In addition to my very smart colleague Rob Wright, who I mentioned, we are thrilled to welcome Lauren Winchester, who is vice president of cyber risk services at Travelers Insurance, and of course Daniel Woods, who is the head of emerging risk at Coalition. Welcome to both of you. Thank you.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

DR's Becky Bracken: This conversation got started actually in one of our editorial meetings, and Rob had the smartest take, and then won the dubious distinction of getting to lead the conversation, which is always a problem around here when you have a smart idea. So, I am going to get out of the way and let Rob explain some of his very smart thinking around this topic, and get you guys in on it.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: It wasn't a smart idea, but it was a question about what is happening with cyber insurance now that we have all this AI stuff going on. Thank you for joining me on this. We'll start with a basic question about where the cyber insurance industry is right now today in 2026, going into 2027. Just broad strokes. I know it's still somewhat of a new market, but where do you feel like it is in terms of overall health and growth? Daniel, why don't you kick us off?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So I think the best data source on the state of the market comes from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, who publish an annual report about the US market, and that shows this paradoxical situation where the number of policies being issued are growing, but the number or the amount of premium being collected is pretty much stable.

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

We also see claims are increasing; they rose 40% in 2024, 20% in 2025. So I think the cyber-insurance market is beginning to ask whether prices are sustainable, especially given some of the changes we'll discuss today related to AI.

DR's Rob Wright: And Lauren, what's your take on what the industry is today?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think we're at a period of uncertainty right now, as most industries are. AI is likely to change a lot of the ways that we work, a lot of the ways that threat actors engage with companies and attack companies, and ultimately that uncertainty is something the industry is grappling with.

DR's Rob Wright: So I know I'm a bit of a pessimist among my Dark Reading colleagues. I try not to be pessimistic, but obviously AI has had a huge effect on the cybersecurity landscape this year. Ever since Project Glasswing, Mythos, and the tsunami of reported vulnerabilities, disclosed vulnerabilities, increases in zero-days. That's really put a lot of companies, a lot of vendors, and enterprises on the defensive. So, what effect is that having?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think it's important not to conflate the surge in vulnerabilities being disclosed with a surge in attacks that drive cyber claims, at least not just yet. As many of your listeners will know, not all vulnerabilities are created equal, and so certainly there are thousands more vulnerabilities being disclosed in the months since Mythos preview came out, as compared to earlier in the year, and that's going to have an impact. And you have to look at the high-severity and the critical bugs within that group, and then you have to look at what's actually being exploited as well.

If we want to look at what's a good stand-in for exploitation, you can look at CISA's known exploited vulnerability list. There's a little lag there, but ultimately, if you look at the KEVs, you can see an increase that's happening, but it's not to the same order of magnitude as the overall CVE and vulnerability disclosure. But certainly, there is an increase. I think we just looked at this recently through Sept. 30, and CISA had added 246 KEVs in 2026, which exceeded the 245 added in total for 2025 when we looked at it. So naturally, we are on a trend to exceed last year.

We think maybe it'll be about a third more than last year, when we get to the end of the year, not a trend you want to see, but it's not in the same almost-exponential curve you're seeing with the total vulnerabilities. And I don't mean to be like everything's fine, right?

We also put out a report yesterday, and we look at ransomware leak site data as well as potential indicators of activity, and that's where ransomware threat actors are posting on their Dark Web leak sites who their victims are, and ultimately for Q3 2026, that activity was up. We had 111 distinct groups posting victims. We had a record number of 2,882 victims on leak sites, which is 26% up from the prior quarter and our highest quarter that we've ever seen. So certainly, the activity with the financially motivated threat actors is picking up, and we've also seen that in our business email compromises (BECs) as well, so it's painting a picture of more activity for sure. But just good to note that increased volumes don't necessarily mean increased tax immediately.

DR's Rob Wright: Gotcha. And I'll just say you are allowed to be positive on this podcast. I am going to actually implore you guys to give me some good news as we get deeper into this conversation because I always try to leave these discussions on a positive note, on a high note, rather than doom and gloom. So, we'll see if Daniel brings the doom and gloom now.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So to bring a bit of gloom, I'd say the conversation also needs to look beyond just vulnerabilities and exploits. AI is a general-purpose technology, and it impacts not just the exploitation of vulnerabilities, but other mechanisms.

So Lauren mentioned an increase in business email compromise, which we've also seen, and we attribute this to in February of this year, a new AI phishing kit was released, EvilTokens, which was basically like a SaaS business model, and they weren't exploiting vulnerabilities. They were using AI to create convincing phishing lures, either by email or often replica websites. They would manipulate the user into letting the attacker in, even if MFA was enforced through either adversary in the middle and phishing, or device code phishing, and then the platform would get access to the mailbox, create mailbox rules, and start to pass through and identify sensitive data.

So this is a way that AI was used at multiple steps. It caused an increase in claims, but it's not actually related to the vulnerabilities that Lauren and you were just talking about. A perfect example. We also attribute that increase in BEC to those tools being made available to threat actors. They are truly too easy to use, unfortunately. EvilTokens was sold as a SaaS business model. So one sophisticated group of criminals built the technology, and they allowed tens, hundreds, thousands of criminals without those skills to use it. And a blockchain tracking company found that they earned $1.1 million in revenue from other criminals buying their services. So, I think this is what Coalition is really worried about when cybercriminals adopt AI into their business models.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We see that in the ransomware ecosystem, where there's ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS), and so part of what we're looking for is when will the tools become even further identified, and to what extent, who will be doing that? Will it be the ransomware developers? How will that actually get disseminated into the ecosystem? There's a little bit more separation between the original, the victims, and who actually ends up doing the attack at the end, because of the access broker economy and what have you. So, I agree with Daniel. You have to track how these different tools are getting used, and to what extent it has changed the ecosystem.

DR's Rob Wright: So I feel like we're trending in a direction that's less positive. That's OK. But going back to the vulnerabilities, do you feel like customers, like the enterprises out there that are buying insurance, are they aware of what's going on with the threat landscape? Do they know about the surge in reported vulnerabilities, and that the patching windows have decreased? That stuff is getting exploited a lot faster these days. That the risk is generally higher, and that there's a much bigger importance to promptly patching systems. Do they understand that, and do you see them acting on it?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: I would say there's a big range of customers. So, of course, at the high end, you have in the enterprise market customers with a team of threat intelligence specialists who don't really need an insurer to tell them about vulnerabilities being exploited. I think where you really see an awareness gap is small businesses. Many of them don't even have an IT team; they have a website some third-party developer built, and then you see something like the PHP vulnerability in that system, and that's where I think the onus is on the insurer to actively notify those customers that there is a new exposure for them. And that's where, in particular, what Coalition offers is support to actually help them patch those systems, because often for the very smallest customers, they don't have the capabilities to do it.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: That's very well put. I think we're definitely doing our darndest to get the news out to our policyholders at Travelers because that is so important. We similarly have a book that runs the gamut from small businesses and mid-sized businesses, and then large enterprises, and the large enterprises are very aware. With middle market and small companies, I do think the work that we've done and other insurers have done to start that engagement before all of this began will hopefully pay off to some extent.

With our cyber-threat alerts, we're letting them know about any of these new emerging exploits, and then certainly in all of our monthly newsletters and quarterly webinars. This is all we can talk about, is how much faster companies need to be patching, and that their 30-day patch windows or SLAs with their vendors are not going to cut it in this new paradigm. They need to be looking to patch within three days, one day, even for certain types of exploits.

But it is interesting you mentioned PHP, not to have a side here, Daniel. But I find that one so fascinating, because the prevalence on the Web. A full 70% of websites could have PHP as a language within them. What do you do with that? You let everybody know about this vulnerability. You encourage everyone to patch, and I actually totally encourage all the press and the news around it because people were patching more quickly on this vulnerability. But turns out it's been pretty hard to exploit so far, right? And so that's a perfect situation for everyone. Something well-known, pervasive, get it fixed, and fortunately beat that exploitation.

DR's Rob Wright: In addition to shrinking patching windows, faster exploitation, and threat actors using AI to build more effective phishing and BEC attacks … what other risks or major threats do you see your clients facing today, as it pertains to AI?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So, I would start with the rise of open source pen-testing frameworks like Artex. This was developed by a Chinese researcher, and it was actually later taken down because the researcher realized how much it was being abused. But what we've seen is this gives, very unsophisticated actors the ability to draw on more sophisticated pen testing tools that have many agents working in parallel to exploit publicly facing systems. What this pen-testing framework is able to do is test systems, test plug-ins, use a range of tools, and basically throw everything at the system and try every avenue, and the costs are so cheap.

For me, the really worrying thing here is often it's just people playing around. They don't even have the rationale on how to make money from this, and yet from a cyber-insurance perspective, you still have to respond to the claim if they steal data, which often happens. You still have to notify those customers. You'll face a lawsuit. So you have just chaos at the moment with these agentic hacking tools being used to just compromise so many different organizations.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: And it's that experimentation that's happening right now. Once the financially motivated threat actors figure out how they want to harness that type of tool, that's when it becomes more concerning. I think right now we're in the early stages of it. That's translated into not seeing much examples of Artex used for ransomware yet, and they tend to be a little noisier right now, so to the point of the large enterprises who are really on top of things, they're going to identify that very quickly within their systems because it's so noisy.

But these tools are only going to get better, and it's something that looks for the existing vulnerabilities that are already out there, the existing exploits, and that's something that every corporation struggles with already. So again, back to the things we've been preaching for so long: needing to make sure you have good vulnerability management and patch management. That's how you combat these new tools. They're not doing net new ways to attack necessarily. They're using existing methods. They're just agentified and moving fast.

But the other risk, if we're talking about other risks from AI, I look at the inside threat of AI as well. here's a real gap between those that know they're adopting AI and those that have AI governance in place, and I think that's really huge. Whenever you have a technological step-change like AI is, adoption is going to get out ahead of governance, and that creates this risk. There's a lack of visibility for a lot of small businesses and middle-market businesses as to how employees are using these tools. There's a lack of accountability. There's a lack of governance. And we're not yet seeing claims and droves that result from this governance gap. But it's happening, and it's creating this risk, and so you can see how companies are going to start to have employees who put sensitive data into an unsanctioned AI tool.

We know that's happening, and that's going to create a potential data breach, depending on what type of information they're putting into the tool. So that's something that when we're engaging with policyholders right now, we're talking to them about vulnerability management, but we're turning around and trying to assess their actual governance risk as well.

DR's Rob Wright: Daniel, are you seeing similar trends in terms of just not necessarily shadow AI usage, but lack of AI governance?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So, I for sure agree with Lauren. There's a bunch of organizations out there using unsanctioned tools. I think to Lauren's point, there's a bunch of data breaches happening that just will never be reported. They will never end up with a breach attorney who says your notification requirements are X, Y, and Z. I think at the moment, Coalition is more sanguine about that risk just because it's remaining in the shadows for now. I think we're really focused on the business email problem because that's causing the spiking claims at the moment, and also how organizations are going to deal with these open source pen-testing frameworks.

DR's Rob Wright: So a question about agentic AI. I've talked with some companies who are trying to find ways to use AI for good, trying to find vulnerabilities within their products, and develop patches in some cases. I spoke with Ivanti about this recently. Do you guys think that that's a realistic path? Have you, or is that a possibility? Like that we may be able to use some of this technology to remedy vulnerabilities, find vulnerabilities, and fix them before the attackers get them, or is that a long way off?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think that's been happening. There are a lot of tech companies that are out ahead of the attackers because they've been running frontier models against their code bases, and then there are also companies that have been running against open source code, right? So there's a plethora of work happening right now to shore up code to ship new patches.

I think one of the problems, though, is for the companies that don't have massive teams who can work on establishing patches. You're told about a new vulnerability. How do you turn around and action that and ship a patch that doesn't have more bugs, right? And so I think that's the spiral we're in right now. There's a bit of a bottleneck, and then companies who are consumers of those tech products then have to do the patches in a lot of cases if it's not a simple cloud update. So, I see this bottleneck happening right now, but it is certainly out ahead of attackers.

That said, some of the models that are out there and in use by attackers now are more sophisticated. So we're at that crux point now, where there are models out there that threat actors can use to identify vulnerabilities and create exploits. And the clock's been ticking, and we're at that intersection.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: Exactly to Lauren's point, there will always be another model that can find new vulnerabilities. Something we're concerned by is, there's been a recent spate of outages. Of course, everyone heard about Microsoft last week. The FAA had an outage, and there's noise that potentially the speed at which organizations are now having to develop and deploy patches is leading to some of these outages. Just because you have to test all of them, and eventually something goes wrong. You test one configuration, then it's pushed to a different server, and that's what causes the outage.

So, although potentially defenders will be able to stay ahead in terms of patching the vulnerabilities, the big concern for cyber insurance is that leads to reliability issues that cause systems failure and business interruptions, which we also cover. So you might solve the security risk, and increase the outage risk.

DR's Rob Wright: I guess the thing I worry about again, and I am a pessimist, so take this with a grain of salt, but is the number of organizations out there that generate the code with AI tools, and push it live without not a lot of human review or really any human review.

And I worry about a future where we're going to have Patch Tuesdays with not just 900 or 1,000 vulnerabilities, but 2,000 or more, and we're just going to be running the code through these AI tools and pushing them out because the sheer number is just too big, and Daniel to your point, not having the quality in place to effectively fix the vulnerability, and also stuff that might screw things up, and you might have outages. That's the panic mode in my brain. Is that something that you guys are worried about, or do you think that we might have the human capability, the human workforce to actually review these patches and the code, and get them in a place that they should be, rather than just pushing them out willy-nilly?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think it's important to not talk about it too broadly, right? Tech companies creating tech have an obligation, a responsibility to have software development lifecycles, so it's one thing to be running AI against the code to test it for vulnerabilities and identify them. You need to make sure you have the proper harnesses in place and the proper engineers and humans overseeing that process, and then you want to run it still before it ships to look for vulnerabilities. You need that life cycle. If they're not doing that, that's creating a real problem. But responsible companies who are creating tech responsibly still have their rigorous software development life cycles in place.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: And I think where I would take that is a similar direction. The cyber insurance industry has seen a huge increase in claims related to SSL VPNs provided by a handful of providers who built them in legacy, proprietary operating systems, they never rewrote those that codebase with modern secure software engineering models. And honestly, I think that business model will always be stuck in this reactive cycle. I think what the insurance industry needs to move toward, and it's something Coalition is doing, is shifting organizations toward a more modern approach to developing software, where you build security in early in the process.

So, for instance, a huge amount of vulnerabilities are related to how memory is managed. There are by now completely memory-safe programming languages that vendors can use to build their systems. So, I think the insurance industry needs to move toward rewarding policyholders who are using more modern technology sets. So, we escape the patch cycle because it's just not sustainable to be telling people at 5 p.m. on a Friday you need to patch your systems. Our staff get exhausted from this because they stay up all night notifying people, and then also the people receiving those emails are just as exhausted.

DR's Rob Wright: You mentioned VPNs. I wanted to ask you guys: so obviously, edge devices have been under attack now for a long time, and there have been specific companies and products that have been favorite targets of threat actors. Lots of vulnerabilities, zero-days, etc. Are carriers or the insurance companies approaching a point where you guys might say to a customer, you know what? If you have this in your environment, the risk is too high for us, and just walk away or say that it's a no-go because of certain edge devices or edge products in that environment? Or are we not there yet?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So I would say, for the vast majority, you can build compensating controls in. So we know SSL VPNs are not great. What we would do is work with the customer to update the firmware to the latest version to enforce multifactor authentication or MFA, and then what we would also ask is whether they have running behind that, a modern managed detection and response solution. So if something gets through, you at least detect it and contain it quickly. It's quite rare that we say there's no way we can insure you. It's more about working with the customer, so they're secure enough to offer terms to.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We take a similar approach as well. We're certainly identifying at the point of underwriting some of the more risky technologies, so that those conversations can be had, those questions can be asked. I'm reaching out to help them understand what a proper patching cadence is going to look like with that edge device that's constantly under attack. What are their plans to move toward something that, in the future, will be more secure? It's not always realistic for a company to move off their VPN quickly, and we recognize that. So it's for those that lean in and say how can I do this securely, and then how can I roadmap to get to where we need to be in the future.

DR's Rob Wright: Last question on AI for you guys. So, we've covered threat actors using AI tools. We've covered the pen testing tools that are available, frameworks, and what it has done to the influx of vulnerabilities. But what about rogue models, agents escaping containment, agents getting into other networks; is that something that you guys have gamed out plans for? Like, if a client is breached by way of an escaped agent, and there's damage or there's data exposed, does it matter who's behind a breach for your customers, or does it become a different calculus when AI is involved?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So, from a coverage perspective, the way cyber insurance policies are worded, the coverage trigger is a security failure, and it's about the victim organization and some unauthorized action being taken on their network.

We never say, we'll cover these kinds of attacks, but not these kinds of attackers. It's always just been about the victim, what did the security incident look like? I don't think this is a coverage conversation.

I think historically the media, and I know we're on a podcast at the moment, has focused on certain kinds of attacks that make great stories, and I think this message that OpenAI was developing a model and it escaped: it makes a great story, but the reality is, for the vast majority of businesses, they're not going to face that kind of threat. I think it's incumbent on cyber insurance to use our data to bring a more sober conversation and focus on how they will actually be compromised: business email compromise, funds transfer fraud, ransomware, and I think that's what we should be helping businesses prevent.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I agree. I think when we talk about the motivations of a rogue agent, it's different than our financially motivated threat actors potentially who are looking to capitalize on that attack. So what that agent does within the environment dictates the response. So, like Daniel said, it doesn't matter if it's a human or an agent. What happened within the environment? What access was had? What data was accessed or exfiltrated or locked up?

I do think, though, there are concerns about agentic use within an organization and when there's agentic drift as well, and that's certainly a known risk, especially among companies that are developing tech. And there are good solutions starting to be built and put into market to help with that monitoring of agents.

But there again, right now in this moment, a lot of companies are lacking that insight and that visibility and that monitoring of agentic behavior, so it's a risk but not something that we're necessarily seeing pronounced in claims yet.

DR's Rob Wright: OK, so let's take a beat and look at 2027. Let's close it out with a look down the road. What do you guys see happening in the next year for the cybersecurity industry, just broadly, Daniel?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: I would expect the increase in frequency of the attacks we've spoken about: business email compromise, phone transfer fraud. The latest evaluations of the very frontier models are finding they can't consistently go from the perimeter of a network to full domain compromise. So I don't think we're going to see automated end-to-end ransomware in 2027. That said, I think there's going to be a lot of chaos, a lot of Web-facing systems breached. They often contain credit-card data, email addresses. So I think it's going to look a lot like the 2010s, more like data breaches, business email compromise.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: If we think about the types of claims that can really drive costs, to what extent are those attacks becoming more and more identified as agentic? Because that necessarily allows threat actors who are financially motivated to have more efficiency and to go after more companies potentially.

Unfortunately, the ransomware threat actors are very successful right now with what they have. And if it ain't broke, don't fix it. So we fully anticipate to see more agentification of different aspects of the attack chain, but that full chaining would be a significant change in this landscape.

DR's Rob Wright: Right. I feel a little bit better about where we are based on what you guys are telling me. Sobering news about how this is going to look more like the 2010s, and we're not going to be having Skynet attacks of rogue agents and models running amok, Daniel. I think you're probably right about that. It's reassuring to hear it. But thank you guys for weighing in on this and giving us a look at what's happening in your industry. Appreciate it.

DR's Becky Bracken: I was going to say, the 2010s don't sound really bad at this point, frankly.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We had some pretty massive data breaches back then, so I wouldn't seem too eager to go back to that pattern.

DR's Becky Bracken: Oh, something about a BlackBerry though just brought me a sense of comfort. I wanted just to ask, because I am infinitely smarter after this conversation than I was on this topic. So thank you all so much, Rob, for your smart questions and Daniel and Lauren. Your wealth of expertise is invaluable. But I want to ask the question that we started off with, which is: are premiums sustainable? Is the cost of cybersecurity insurance in its current stratosphere, is it sustainable? And what is going to happen with costs in your estimation?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: I don't think the current trend is sustainable, and I think premiums will have to go up. If there are more claims, there are more costs. Insurers need to collect the premiums to cover it.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: And I think that statement was true prior to the frontier AI models. So a lot of insurers within the industry are definitely feeling that that struggle with the current levels of premiums and the current view of risk.

DR's Rob Wright: Although I gotta say, you would think they'd be much higher than they are right now. So I guess that's good. I can't believe I'm being an optimist right now.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: There are other market conditions at play. There are a lot of markets that are selling cyber, and there are new entrants, and that has an impact.

DR's Becky Bracken: Again, you guys have left us all with a lot to think about, from the governance gap to the speed up of patching introducing configuration problems. I think that we're going to be thinking a lot about all of this in the future.

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition; Lauren Winchester, head of cyber risk services at Travelers Insurance; and Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading: thank you all so much for your time and your expertise today, we appreciate it. This has been Dark Reading Confidential, a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken, on behalf of all of us at Dark Reading. Thank you so much for tuning in, and we will see you or hear you next time. Bye.

The Dark Reading Editorial Team consists of Kelly Jackson Higgins, Fahmida Y Rashid, Tara Seals, Rob Wright, Becky Bracken, Alex Culafi, Arielle Waldman, and Kristina Beek. #9780. We Swapped Our MCP Server's Base Image and Went From 36 Reported Vulnerabilities to Zero

Abhimanyu Garg is a Staff Software Engineer, DevOps/SRE working on CI/CD developer velocity, Kubernetes resiliency, observability and agentic AIOps.

Senior Site Reliability & DevOps Engineer | Docker | AWS, Kubernetes, Pulumi, Security & Compliance | CI/CD Automation Expert

Abhimanyu Garg is a Staff Software Engineer, DevOps/SRE working on CI/CD developer velocity, Kubernetes resiliency, observability and agentic AIOps.

Senior Site Reliability & DevOps Engineer | Docker | AWS, Kubernetes, Pulumi, Security & Compliance | CI/CD Automation Expert

Abhimanyu Garg is a Staff Software Engineer, DevOps/SRE working on CI/CD developer velocity, Kubernetes resiliency, observability and agentic AIOps.

Senior Site Reliability & DevOps Engineer | Docker | AWS, Kubernetes, Pulumi, Security & Compliance | CI/CD Automation Expert

We run a small internal tool a custom MCP server, the kind of thing more teams are now standing up to give AI agents access to internal systems like GitHub or Slack. It runs as a container, same as everything else. We hadn’t scrutinized its base image the way we would a customer-facing service, mostly because it never occurred to us that it needed the same level of attention. So we migrated it from a standard base image to a hardened one and measured what actually changed, rather than assuming the usual advice about “minimal images” applied here the way it does everywhere else.

Both builds used the same application source and declared dependencies (package.json, src/); the runtime base changed from Debian-based Node (node:24-trixie-slim) to Alpine-based Docker Hardened Images (dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.23), built via a multi-stage Dockerfile with a -dev variant for the build stage. Both images were scanned with Docker Scout on September 28, 2026, on the same architecture (linux/amd64). Because the distribution changed along with the image provider, treat the numbers below as a comparison of these two specific builds, not an isolated measurement of what hardening alone contributes some of the difference reflects Alpine’s smaller footprint relative to Debian, independent of the hardening effort itself.

This is a single migration of a single tool, not a controlled study across image types treat it as one documented data point, not a general verdict on any vendor's product.

Everything needed to reproduce this is public in the hardened-mcp-server repository: the MCP server source, both Dockerfiles, and the GitHub Actions workflow that builds, smoke-tests and scans each image. The numbers below come from one CI run on September 28, 2026.

Vulnerabilities reported by Docker Scout, Sept 28, 2026

36 (0 Critical / 6 High / 6 Medium / 24 Low)

Note: Docker Scout’s size report for the standard image is 104 MB but plain docker images lists it as 255 MB. For the hardened image, Docker Scout lists it as 56 MB but plain docker images lists it as 135 MB. The gap is expected: docker images shows the uncompressed size on local disk, while Docker Scout reports the compressed size.

The hardened build is a two-stage Dockerfile. The -dev tag includes a shell and npm, so dependencies are installed there. The runtime stage uses the plain tag, which has no shell, and only receives the files the server needs to run.

Pulling from dhi.io needs a free Docker ID and a one-time docker login dhi.io. DHI tags change on Docker’s own schedule, so check the DHI catalog for current tags before copying these.

The package-count reduction did not mostly consist of obscure OS packages. Instead many of the removed packages were from the npm toolchain itself, e.g. @npmcli/arborist, pacote, npm-registry-fetch, etc. These packages are part of the standard Node.js image but the MCP server never runs npm in production, only node src/server.js. Thus they represent attack surface for code that never runs anyway, and a hardened base image removes them as a side effect of its minimal nature.

The rest was the Debian userland the server never touches at runtime: bash, systemd, login/passwd/shadow, pam, sysvinit, apt and dpkg.

Hardened runtime images are typically shipped without a shell but every major option here also ships a debug or development variant precisely so you're not left without one when you need it: distroless publishes :debug tags with a busybox shell, Chainguard offers :latest-dev tags with a full toolchain, and Docker Hardened Images has -dev variants we used exactly this variant for our own build stage, because Docker's RUN instruction executes through a shell by default and the build stage needs to run npm ci. The practical takeaway isn't "accept no shell, ever" it's choosing a minimal variant for the production runtime and deliberately planning a separate debugging path in advance, rather than assuming the shell you're used to having will still be there when something breaks.

For Docker Hardened Images specifically, Docker Debug attaches a debugging toolkit to a running container without adding a shell to the image itself, so docker exec -it sh failing is no longer a dead end.

Google’s distroless images are built on top of Debian and are automatically updated to the latest Debian packages via pull requests to the distroless repository. Chainguard builds packages from source on top of its own distribution, Wolfi, and builds images daily with pinned versions of packages. Hardened versions of Docker images are built on top of the Debian or Alpine Linux distributions and are free and Apache 2.0 licensed as of the end of 2025. This means that, depending on your existing toolchain, the compliance requirements of your organization, and how much effort you are willing to invest in migrating, there is a hardened image provider that can fit your needs.

The container that needed hardening used to be almost always customer-facing. Increasingly, it's internal tooling too MCP servers, agent bridges, anything giving an AI system reach into company systems. Those containers carry real credentials and real API access, and in our own experience, this class of internal tooling hasn't gotten the same scanning rigor as public-facing services. That's the actual gap this exercise closed for us: not a security guarantee, but a measurable, documented reduction in attack surface for one of these newer, less-scrutinized internal services.

Abhimanyu Garg is a Staff Software Engineer, DevOps/SRE working on CI/CD developer velocity, Kubernetes resiliency, observability and agentic AIOps.

Senior Site Reliability & DevOps Engineer | Docker | AWS, Kubernetes, Pulumi, Security & Compliance | CI/CD Automation Expert

#9779. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

#9778. It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Bot detection has become a losing game. Security teams need to limit privileged access for humans and their machine counterparts equally.

The Internet is flooded with bots. People use them to organize their emails, shop, chat, and handle some of their busywork.

At the other end of the spectrum sit attackers who want to increase their speed just as much as, if not more than, legitimate users. The faster they can conduct distributed denial-of-service attacks or brute-force password attacks, the quicker they can breach an organization and the more victims they can claim.

The line between legitimate and illegitimate activity grows finer by the minute, as bots have become pros at mirroring human behavior — even its flaws. For example, during the infamous incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, bots reportedly found ways to communicate with one another by accessing the outside Internet — something they weren't programmed to do.

Behavioral baselines that security teams once relied on are becoming moot, since bots can impersonate humans. As the volume of bots accelerates, the real question isn't human versus bot but what that activity is telling teams and how to police it.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Security tools will miss something, so teams should choose systems that allow them to quickly edit, adjust, and continually adapt to a changing environment, explains Jeremy London, director of engineering, AI, and threat analytics at Keeper Security.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents, which can perform automated actions similar to bots without human oversight, are only adding to environmental complexities. While some advancements can be exciting, they also introduce more gaps and zero-day vulnerabilities to the attack surface that "we just didn't understand," London says.

"I think the continual effort, as a security organization, is to show up with the right tooling, understand what you're trying to solve for, and then be able to react quickly because your control plane probably missed something — that's a guarantee," London tells Dark Reading.

Organizations underwent significant transformations over the past decade, propelled by AI. Adoption moved at a scale that "no one ever predicted," London says. That has forced teams to cut corners on important safeguards.

Code reviews and security practices need a serious makeover, especially regarding boundaries and compliance. Bots and agents have new levels of autonomy and access, leading to more unpredictability and changing what security risks even look like.

However, such a makeover has proved to be a difficult undertaking because AI doesn't come with a security playbook, London explains. A decade ago, bots were rigid and scripts performed a single action. Now "teams vibe code stuff and throw things at the wall and see what works, and the scale that [bots] can operate at is totally different," he says.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

While organizations struggle, attackers are having a field day with these advancements. Given all of the recent disclosures and reports, it's no surprise that attacks are rising. What is surprising is how quickly threat actors can adapt and respond to countermeasures, says Jérôme Segura, VP of threat research at DataDome, a bot management and agent trust platform.

"Anytime we put challenges in front of them, we see it slows them down and costs them more because to run the same operation, they have to use more resources, which becomes expensive," he explains.

The reason the attackers aren't giving up despite the obstacles is that their attacks are working, Segura tells Dark Reading.

"Because the payout is so great, they're doubling, tripling their investments," he says.

The persistence is challenging and frustrating for defenders. But it's just the stark reality that threat actors are highly motivated, and "we're battling against that," Segura adds.

When threat actors use bots against online retailers, they replicate the exact flow of a human but without all the telltale signs, such as hesitating over a purchasing decision, fumbling to enter card or shipping details, or pausing to solve a CAPTCHA challenge. They don't need to click through every page like a human would or wait for the site to load all the images either. As a result, bots complete transactions in a split second, Segura says. The speed can create security risks and unfair competition for legitimate users.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

More concerningly, bots complete these tasks in ways that appear legitimate because they're aware that companies are trying to block this malicious activity, he says. And the volume is only increasing. Segura conducted research analyzing traffic hitting retailers' product pages and found that 91% were actually bad bots.

Taking legal action is difficult when it's nearly impossible to differentiate legitimate and illegitimate activity, which puts even more pressure on businesses. Scraping product pages or ticket scalping remains "kind of a gray area in terms of the legal aspect," Segura explains, adding that the law isn't quite clear yet on what is permitted.

In some cases, the culprits are organized groups just looking to make money and oftentimes use loopholes to circumvent the law. For example, they end up using existing infrastructure to collect scarce products and resell them, Segura says.

Threat actors organize so that they have specialties, just as defenders do, he has observed. Some specialize in reverse engineering specific parts of a website's code to understand how it works. Others focus on providing the necessary infrastructure, including all the IP addresses, to carry out those kinds of attacks, he says.

"You can source IPs from real users that are extremely convincing because they're also shared by humans," Segura explains. "So all these specializations within these groups, working well together, and making sure everybody's getting paid, is really interesting."

Behavioral analytics are struggling right now, London says, and is a "pain point" rippling across the industry.

Some bots can move the mouse pointer and send keystrokes to mimic typing, so verification techniques like measuring mouse movements or typing speeds need to evolve. Models can be a bit slow, just as humans can be, he notes.

"Although they are robotic in nature, some of those behavioral or human factors that teams have been using for indication points are really close," London says.

Since it's so difficult to determine whether activity is from a human or a bot, organizations should manage them both the same way when it comes to privileged identity: the less access, the better.

Given all of the risks and potential blast radii, "security teams, not developers, should probably decide whether AI is allowed in an organization," London recommends.

"From a security perspective, it makes it somewhat simple because AI agents can do bad things [and] humans can do bad things," he says. "So if we just look at it through that perspective, I don't care if it's a human or an agent."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9777. Why Topscan.me Stopped Counting Vulnerabilities and Started Scoring Its SLA

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

The Security Score on Topscan.me's dashboard used to move the wrong way when a team looked harder. Switch a workspace from monthly scans to weekly, or finally point the scanner at the staging box nobody had touched in two years, and the number at the top of the screen would fall. Security had not changed that morning. Only the visible part of the estate had grown, and the model read visibility as damage.

The company rebuilt the model earlier this year. The technical detail here comes from Topscan's Chief Product Officer, Aleksandr Melnichuk.

The original Security Score was a deduction model in the plainest sense. Start at 100. Subtract a weight for every open finding, scaled by severity. Subtract more for anything already past its remediation deadline. Cap the total so a large backlog could not drive the figure to zero, and display the result as a 0-100 health number that a CTO could put in front of a board.

The logic is hard to argue with in the abstract. Fewer open vulnerabilities is better than more, and critical ones should weigh more than low ones.

Once it ran on real workspaces, the score turned out to move when nothing had changed. Import a set of AWS assets, or run a discovery pass that surfaces subdomains from a campaign site nobody remembers owning, and the score drops the same day. Those vulnerabilities were there the whole time. Finding them is progress, and the model logged it as decline.

Worse, it rewarded not looking, and this is the part that decided the rewrite. If open findings cost points, the cheapest way to hold a good score is to scan less often and leave the awkward hosts off the target list. Nobody sits down and plans that. The incentive is there anyway.

And it could not tell whether anyone was keeping their promises. A workspace with 200 findings, every one of them inside its remediation window and moving, was charged for all 200. A workspace with a dozen findings that had been ignored for six weeks was charged for twelve, plus the overdue surcharge, so the team doing the work was charged for far more findings than the team with the shorter list.

"A score that drops when you scan more is not measuring security. It is measuring how much you have admitted to," says Melnichuk. "We had shipped a score that paid people to look away. Once you notice that, you cannot really leave it alone."

One rule carries the whole model: a finding resolved inside its deadline costs nothing at all, not even a small deduction.

The score only starts to drop when a finding passes the deadline attached to its severity, and from that day the penalty grows for as long as the finding stays open. Severity sets how heavy the penalty is, so a critical past its date costs considerably more than a low. Once a rescan no longer detects the finding, Topscan marks it fixed, the penalty stops and the score climbs back.

The deadlines are the defaults listed on the Topscan.me vulnerability management page: critical in 7 days, high in 30, medium in 60, low in 90. The timer starts at first detection, not at the most recent scan and not at the moment somebody created a ticket. A finding still detected in later scans keeps its original deadline.

Consider a workspace with 140 open findings across a wide estate. The oldest was first seen nine days ago and carries a 30-day window. Nothing is past its date. That workspace scores 100.

A second workspace has eleven open findings, three of them critical and first detected five weeks ago. It loses points, and keeps losing more until someone fixes or snoozes those criticals.

The scanning incentive flips along with it. Detection is free now. Pointing the scanner at a forgotten host costs zero points on the day you find whatever is running on it, and hands you a full remediation window to deal with it.

Goodhart's law is the standard warning here: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. In vulnerability management**,** it takes a very specific shape. If the metric punishes overdue work, and a team has a finding they genuinely cannot fix this month because the vendor has not shipped a patch or the deployment window is two weeks out, then the metric is quietly pushing them to close the ticket and move on.

So the model needs a legitimate way to say "not now", or it will get an illegitimate one.

The model also declines to charge teams for things that are not their work. Informational findings with no CVE attached are classed as noise and never counted. A finding marked as a false positive drops out of scoring and out of SLA tracking entirely, though if a later scan sees it again it returns to the current list, on the theory that something on the target may have changed since the last time a human judged it.

"Every metric a team is measured on has a cheat code, and the design question is which one you hand them," Melnichuk says. "I would much rather someone press snooze with a date on it than close a ticket that is not fixed. One of those keeps the finding on the board."

Melnichuk's list of what the score misses starts with coverage, which the score says nothing about. A workspace scanning three assets out of forty can hold a perfect 100 while being blind to most of its own perimeter. Topscan chose not to patch that hole from inside the score, on the grounds that folding coverage into the same figure would have made both halves unreadable. Scan coverage sits next to the score as its own number: targets scanned in the last 30 days against total targets.

"You can get a hundred by scanning three things and fixing them on time. That is the obvious hole in it," Melnichuk says. "We left it visible instead of hiding it in the formula. A single figure that quietly folds in everything stops being checkable, and a number nobody can check does not survive contact with an auditor."

Severity still comes from CVSS. A CVSS base score describes how bad a flaw would be if exploited, and on its own it says nothing about whether anyone is exploiting it on infrastructure like yours. The product surfaces a separate exploit-known flag for findings with a working public exploit, and in day-to-day triage that flag deserves more weight than a CVSS band does. The wider industry is moving the same way. CISA's BOD 26-04, issued in June 2026, revoked the older directive that tied federal civilian agencies' patch deadlines to CVSS severity and replaced it with a decision table built from four facts about each finding: whether the asset is publicly exposed, whether the CVE is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, how automatable the attack is, and how much control a successful attack hands over. EPSS, which estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days, pushes the same way. Topscan's score has not caught up with that yet: it weighs severity and lateness, and exploit-known findings are flagged separately.

Two decisions in this story go further than the arithmetic.

The first is choosing what the metric charges for, because that is what its users will optimize whether or not anyone meant them to. Topscan's charges for missed promises. Discovery is free, and so is a backlog that grew because somebody finally looked. By Melnichuk's account that single choice changed more behavior than any weighting adjustment did.

The second is designing the exception before shipping, before somebody games the metric. A deferral path bolted on later tends to arrive as a workaround with a feature name. The pause exists because a real team, on a real Tuesday, will have a finding they cannot fix yet and a number they are being judged on.

The count did not disappear, incidentally. Open criticals and highs still sit on the dashboard, one panel over, where they tell you what to open first. They no longer set the headline number.

The current model is described in Topscan's help center. Quotes and the account of the earlier model come from an interview with Aleksandr Melnichuk, Chief Product Officer at Topscan.me.

#9776. Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

Researchers discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages as part of a fake recruitment campaign that spreads malware and gives attackers access to developers' machines.

A coordinated supply chain campaign is targeting .NET developers with fake coding assignments, weaponized software dependencies, and GitHub-hosted malware capable of stealing browser credentials and establishing remote access.

Researchers at Socket discovered the campaign, which involves 13 malicious NuGet packages designed to compromise Windows-based developer environments through seemingly legitimate job assessments, according to a report published this week. The packages use fake job "Home Assessment" projects to target Windows .NET developers, with most posing as button controls for WinUI 3 and WPF, which are user interface frameworks for building applications.

"In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL side-loading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable," Socket researcher Kush Pandya wrote in the report.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

As in similar campaigns that weaponize developer repositories and code packages, attackers are exploiting developers' willingness to download, build, and run code they believe to be trustworthy. In this case, the malicious code is disguised as part of job-recruitment exercises for .NET developers. Such campaigns can turn routine development activities into infection vectors, potentially spreading malware and malicious code through the software supply chain.

NuGet is a package manager for .NET. Socket researchers traced the campaign across NuGet, GitHub repositories, and malicious code embedded in development projects, identifying packages linked through shared attack infrastructure and techniques.

The most recent example they found was a GitHub repository created on Nov. 4 that contained a purported WinUI 3 assessment called "Mini File Vault & Tracker." The project instructed candidates to complete a three- to four-hour development exercise using a supplied Visual Studio project. However, its dependencies contained malicious code.

"Candidates are told that building the project shows the starter UI and that the work must be developed and tested on native Windows with Visual Studio 2026," Pandya wrote in the report.

Socket could not determine how the Home Assessment lures reached candidates, as researchers found "no recruiter message, email or job post for them," he added.

The attack involved two malicious NuGet packages working together. One executed code after every project build, while the other launched a staged executable when the application created its button control. This effectively turned an ordinary development workflow into an infection chain.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

The investigation eventually uncovered 13 unique package names and 28 versions across those packages, as well as four NuGet publisher accounts linked to the operation.

Characterizing the campaign as posing a very serious threat to enterprises, Pandya says attackers could gain access to a "treasure trove" of sensitive information by compromising a developer's machine.

"A developer's machine holds source code, SSH keys, GitHub, package registry and cloud tokens, and browser sessions that have often already passed multifactor authentication," Pandya tells Dark Reading. "In this campaign, building the take-home project was enough to run the threat actor's code."

Beyond access to terminals and configuration files, many developers who work from a console have their command history automatically collected, he says. This can give adversaries insight into the commands developers have executed, as well as access to passwords and API keys that may have been inadvertently pasted into the command line, he adds.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Moreover, by disguising their activity as legitimate development work, attackers gain a degree of stealth and control once the malicious code is running on a developer's machine, he says.

"A threat actor could extract SSH keys and network configurations, but their access is still from an external host and must go through various security controls," Pandya explains. "If they are working directly from a developer's machine, they not only have the necessary access keys but also the expected IP address and geolocation to avoid suspicion."

As adversaries continue to weaponize code packages from legitimate sources to compromise the software supply chain, developers and security teams must remain vigilant. Socket has recommendations for both.

Developers should treat take-home coding assignments and unfamiliar projects as untrusted code, Pandya advises. Before building them, they should check for unfamiliar NuGet dependencies, additional package sources, and build scripts that could execute automatically.

"Open take-home tests and unfamiliar repositories only in a disposable virtual machine with no credentials," he recommends. "Restrict which package sources projects can use, scan dependencies before they are installed, and verify recruiters through official channels."

Organizations should also restrict which NuGet feeds developers can use and review third-party packages that contain build scripts capable of executing commands, according to Socket. They should also educate employees and job candidates about fake recruitment assessments to reduce the risk of attackers exploiting the hiring process to gain access to developer environments.

Security teams, meanwhile, should identify affected developer machines and treat suspected infections as potential credential and software supply chain compromises, rather than simply malware incidents, Pandya says.

"If a machine is compromised, isolate and reimage it, rotate credentials and tokens from a clean device, revoke active sessions, and review audit logs," he says.
