#9775. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9774. Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

A previously undocumented Iranian threat group called "Volant Manticore" is targeting Cypriot organizations as part of an intelligence-gathering effort for Tehran.

Cyprus' growing security ties with Israel and its use as a staging ground for Western forces operating across the Middle East appear to be making the island an increasingly attractive target for Iranian cyber espionage.

Volant Manticore is an early example of that interest. The previously undocumented advanced persistent threat (APT) group has been targeting organizations in Cyprus as part of what researchers at Check Point describe as an Iranian intelligence-gathering campaign focused on the island.

Its targets so far have included a Cyprus-based airline operating primarily between Cyprus and Israel, telecommunications providers, critical infrastructure organizations, and a suspected government entity with military connections. The selection of targets suggests an effort to gather intelligence on the island's government, infrastructure, and relationships with regional partners, the researchers said.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

Check Point has assessed with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is likely an offshoot of the Iranian threat group MuddyWater, tasked primarily with spying on Cypriot organizations on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). It is among the first known Iranian groups to have a dedicated focus on Cyprus, although it has recently expanded its targeting to organizations in Saudi Arabia, says Sergey Shykevich, director of threat intelligence at Check Point Software.

"Cyprus' defense and energy ties with Israel and Greece, along with its role in Western military operations in the region, may help explain why it is a target for intelligence gathering," Shykevich says.

He points to a Check Point report from earlier this year on a surge in attempts by Iran-linked actors to exploit vulnerabilities in Internet-connected surveillance cameras across the Middle East, including Cyprus, beginning on Feb. 28, when US and Israeli strikes against Iran began. Access to the cameras could have provided Iranian intelligence with a way to monitor military and other strategically important facilities, gather information ahead of potential attacks, and assess the damage from strikes afterward. "The timing is another indication of how Iranian cyber activity tracks with security developments in the region," Shykevich adds.

Check Point described Volant Manticore as relying heavily on phishing to gain an initial foothold using lures tailored for the organizations and sectors it targets. The security vendor's investigation of the group began when it spotted a fabricated resume on VirusTotal associated with "Athena Marinou," a fictitious, AI-generated travel-and-tourism professional.

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

The document directed recipients to download the full CV from what appeared to be a legitimate recruitment website. The link, however, pointed to an archive hosted on Catbox, which delivered KuboShell — a custom backdoor that the group is using to establish an initial foothold on compromised systems, conduct basic reconnaissance, and receive commands from its operators.

Check Point found that the Windows-based backdoor uses the decentralized InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) communications, potentially making them harder to block or disrupt than communications routed through a conventional attacker-controlled server. The malware allows attackers to collect details about compromised systems and networks using basic PowerShell instructions. Check Point found evidence that the group then deployed a more extensive, multistage post-compromise toolkit it calls the Homa Framework.

Volant Manticore also uses legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software such as N-able, NetLock, and MeshCentral in its campaigns. The tools enable remote access and administrative capabilities while allowing the attacks to blend in with legitimate traffic. Check Point also identified infrastructure associated with credential-harvesting campaigns, including domains designed to resemble corporate email services. The researchers found evidence of operators testing their malware against antivirus products and using virtual machines and VPN-related software in their operational environments.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

Check Point's analysis showed overlaps between Volant Manticore's techniques and code and those used by the long-active Iranian group MuddyWater. However, Check Point assessed Volant Manticore is a separate operation likely run by former MuddyWater members. "The group has a well-developed toolkit that combines techniques we’ve seen from MuddyWater with tools it developed itself," Shykevich says. "One of the less common techniques we observed was its use of KuboShell, a backdoor that provides remote access and communicates through IPFS, a decentralized file-sharing network."

In September, Check Point observed the group suddenly broadening its focus to include Saudi Arabia. "We are currently seeing the group active in both countries," Shykevich says. While Cyprus remains its primary espionage target, the group has been targeting Saudi organizations as well, mainly in the healthcare sector, he adds. "The increase in activity coincided with escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The scale of the group's activity in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere is likely to vary as the situation in the region evolves."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9773. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9772. Off-Grid Messaging with MeshCore: How to Text When the Cell Towers Go Dark

A beginner's guide to MeshCore LoRa mesh radios: how they work, which hardware to buy, and how to fix the classic problem where you can hear the mesh but it can't hear you.

I have a weakness for radios that nobody needs permission to use. In a previous life, I braved 5°F winter days scanning public Wi-Fi all over downtown Helsinki, warmed by nothing but spiked glögg. Wi-Fi taught me that a little unlicensed spectrum and a lot of clever engineering can change the world. Ham radio taught me that the best communications gear is the kind that still works when everything else has given up. So when I found a $40 radio that could text people miles away, with no towers, no SIM card and no license, I had a new hobby before I'd finished reading the product page.

It also exposed a blind spot in my emergency kit. Water: check. Forty pounds of freeze-dried lasagna: check. Hand-crank flashlight that doubles as a phone charger: check. And under Communications, a phone. A phone that is, in practice, a very expensive flashlight once the nearest cell tower loses power.

Off-grid mesh networking fills that gap: cheap long-range radios that form their own text network, with no carrier in sight. I spent the past couple of months on the Bay Area's MeshCore network with a handful of radios, one SDR dongle, and more patience than I knew I had. For ten frustrating days I could hear the whole mesh, and it couldn't hear me. This guide covers what I wish I'd known on day one: why people do this, how MeshCore works, what to buy, and how to fix the problem almost every beginner hits.

Modern communication is a long chain of things that need electricity and a business model: towers, backhaul fiber, data centers, and the goodwill of your carrier. Break any link and your $1,200 slab of glass is reduced to playing the offline games you never installed.

After Hurricane Helene in September 2024, parts of western North Carolina lost power and cell service for days, in places for weeks. In April 2025, the Iberian blackout took mobile service down across Spain and Portugal within hours, once tower backup batteries ran dry.

In the Bay Area, I don't have to imagine it. We have earthquake faults under our feet and fire seasons that bring planned PG&E power shutoffs. On October 27, 2019, high winds, a forest fire and a PG&E shutoff took out my power, internet and cable TV all at once. The Mercury News wrote about it, and I ended up building a cardboard-and-tinfoil antenna to watch Sunday football over the air.

Mesh radios don't care. They run for days on a small battery, indefinitely on a palm-sized solar panel, and relay messages through each other instead of through a tower.

First, a naming hazard. LoRa (lowercase a, "Long Range") is a radio modulation owned by Semtech. It has nothing to do with LoRA, the AI fine-tuning trick. I spend a lot of time around AI people, and I can confirm that search engines find this hilarious.

LoRa uses chirp spread spectrum: each symbol is a tone sweeping across a slice of spectrum. Because the receiver knows the shape of the chirp, it can dig a signal out from below the noise floor. That's how a radio putting out about as much power as a phone's Wi-Fi reaches miles instead of yards.

The trade-off is bandwidth: a few hundred bits to a few kilobits per second. Enough for a text or a GPS position, never enough for a photo of your dog. LoRa runs in unlicensed ISM bands: 915 MHz in the Americas and Australia/New Zealand, 868 MHz in Europe and the UK. Sub-gigahertz signals pass through trees, walls and San Francisco fog far better than Wi-Fi. Karl the Fog is not the problem. The hills are.

A cell network is a star: lose the tower and everyone in range goes silent. A mesh has no center. Radios pass messages along, hop by hop, until they arrive.

Cellular and Wi-Fi depend on someone else's infrastructure. Ham radio doesn't, but it takes an exam, real skill, and (in most countries) a ban on encryption. LoRa mesh is what I'd hand to my non-radio-nerd family: no license, encrypted, days on a battery, and it looks like a messaging app.

Both big projects run on the same cheap LoRa boards. They're different firmware with opposite ideas about who should relay.

The honest verdict: for a group that moves around together and wants something that works out of the box, pick Meshtastic. If your city has MeshCore repeaters, or you want to help build permanent regional coverage, pick MeshCore.

Around the Bay, the second case is winning.

That's what a mesh looks like when it delivers reliably enough for real conversation. The Bay Area MeshCore crowd has put hundreds of repeaters on rooftops, hilltops and the occasional tree. One of my test messages was heard by 66 of them, across a span of 238 miles. The two networks can't talk to each other, so the right choice is whichever one your neighbors run. Mine run MeshCore.

MeshCore's design fits on a napkin. There are three kinds of node:

Every node has a cryptographic key pair, and the public key is its identity: no accounts, servers or phone numbers. Nodes introduce themselves with an advert, a signed packet carrying their public key, a name, and optionally a location. Repeaters advert every 12 hours. Companions advert only when you tell them to, so press that button when you're new, or nobody will know you exist.

A flood packet gets repeated by anyone who hasn't already; a direct one only by the next repeater on its path. Repeaters forward your words but can't read them.

Alice in Berkeley texts Bob in San Jose. Both have advertised, so each has the other's public key.

If the route breaks (say, a repeater loses power), Alice's radio retries three times and floods the last attempt to find a new route.

Group channels always flood, because "everyone in #test" has no single destination. A channel is just a shared key. Public uses a well-known key, and a #hashtag channel's key is derived from its name, so anyone who guesses the name can read along. Treat both as billboards.

Two honest caveats. The cryptography is lean (tiny authentication tags, no forward secrecy): fine for a camping trip, not for a nation-state threat model. And with only 256 possible 1-byte repeater IDs, busy regions get collisions, which is why the Bay Area mesh is moving to 2-byte IDs.

Check official support before you buy. My first rig was an M5Stack Cardputer ADV, a credit-card-sized computer with a keyboard, plus the snap-on Cap LoRa-1262 radio with GPS. Meshtastic supports it officially. MeshCore didn't, so I ended up writing my own MeshCore firmware for it (it's on M5Burner as Bruce's MeshCore, if you have one). Fun hobby, not a beginner's path. Before buying anything, find your board in the MeshCore web flasher. If it isn't listed, you're on your own.

Decide how you want to type. Bluetooth companions are small boards paired to the MeshCore phone app: cheap, simple, and the app is good. But your phone becomes part of the system, and in a real outage you'll want its battery for other things. Standalone devices have their own screen and keyboard and need no phone at all. That's what I'd want in a go-bag.

Battery life depends on the chip. Radios built on Nordic's nRF52 chips sip power, often running a week or more on a small battery. ESP32 radios are more capable but hungrier: with the screen off, my Cardputer draws 120–150 mA, so its 1,500 mAh battery lasts 10–12 hours, not days. For something that sits in a bag listening, nRF52 wins.

GPS costs more than battery life. On my radio, the running GPS receiver raised the LoRa noise floor by about 4 dB, making it measurably deafer. Keep GPS off unless you actually need your position.

Newest isn't always best. I tested a brand-new radio built on Semtech's fourth-generation LR2021 chip (most radios use the second-generation SX1262). On a cheap SDR dongle it showed two problems: it sent the start of each packet about 25 dB too quietly, and it sat 23 kHz off frequency. The first turned out to be a firmware bug, which I've since patched in my own build. The second happens because the board has no TCXO (a temperature-compensated crystal), which matters on MeshCore's narrow 62.5 kHz channels. Prefer boards with a TCXO, and let other people beta-test the shiny new silicon.

Get an external antenna connector. You'll want to upgrade the antenna (see section 7), so look for SMA or RP-SMA, not a tiny internal antenna.

Buy two radios. It sounds greedy, but a second, known-good radio is the best diagnostic tool you'll ever own. It's how I proved my problem wasn't my hardware.

If I were starting over, I'd get a LilyGO T-Deck Plus with the community-built WadaMesh firmware, which is much nicer to use than the official T-Deck build. It looks like a BlackBerry that took up survivalism: thumb keyboard, trackball, 2.8-inch touchscreen, GPS, a 2,000 mAh battery and an SX1262 radio with a TCXO. No phone required. It was also my known-good reference through every test in this article.

Buy the right band for your region: 915 MHz for the Americas and ANZ, 868 MHz for Europe and the UK. Buying the wrong one is the hobby's most common rite of passage.

For everything else, start from the Bay Area MeshCore recommended devices list. It's written by the people who run the repeaters and is refreshingly honest about weak spots. Condensed, with my pick on top:

My go-bag pick. Keyboard, screen, GPS, battery; no phone needed.

Best-value starter: screen, GPS, battery, external antenna. About 5 days per charge. Ships with MeshCore.

3D-printed case, not waterproof. Upgrade the antenna.

Complete kit with case, GPS and OLED. Strong transmit power, which helps you get heard.

ESP32, so shorter battery life. Not waterproof.

The classic: e-ink screen, great battery life, lots of community know-how.

Weak stock antenna, small battery, fragile buttons.

Not a first device. Sealed antenna hears well but struggles to be heard.

5 W solar panel, big battery, reportedly two weeks without sun.

Swap the 2 dBi stock antenna. Not IP-rated.

Smaller panel and battery. RP-SMA connector.

Prices from the Bay Area MeshCore list, last updated March 2026. Most of these ship with Meshtastic; flash MeshCore once when it arrives.

Notice the pattern: almost every entry says "upgrade the antenna." It's usually the single biggest improvement you can make, and the first fix for the lopsided-link problem in section 7. Check that the connector (SMA, RP-SMA or N-type) matches your device, or order an adapter too.

Pro tip: never power on a LoRa radio without an antenna attached. Transmitting into nothing can fry the radio chip, a lesson almost everyone learns once.

MeshCore lives or dies by repeaters, so check there's a network before you spend a cent.

A few radios, like the Wio Tracker L1 Pro, arrive with MeshCore installed; most ship with Meshtastic. Either way, flash the latest release. No soldering and no compiler, just a USB cable and Chrome. Open flasher.meshcore.io, pick your board, and pick a role: Companion for your pocket radio, Repeater for the roof. Bluetooth companions then pair with the MeshCore phone app.

Set your region preset (this is the legal part, so don't skip it), press advert so others can find you, and send your first message. Mine was "Hi" on Public. Nobody replied to this clueless newbie. As it turned out, nobody had heard him.

This is the most common beginner problem in MeshCore. It cost me ten days.

Your radio fills up with repeaters and messages. But anything you send disappears: channel messages never come back as repeats, DMs never show as delivered, and nobody replies. It feels like a broken transmitter. It almost never is.

Radio paths work the same in both directions, but the two ends of the link don't:

The upshot: being 4–6 dB short of the nearest repeater is enough to lose most of your sends. That's less than the difference between your desk and your window.

Like any engineer, I blamed my gear and spent a week swapping settings, firmware and suspicions about every component on the board. Two things finally cracked it.

First, a known-good reference. I bought a T-Deck Plus, and it failed from my house too. Then I used a cheap RTL-SDR dongle as a crude power meter, with both radios taking turns on the same marked spot. My Cardputer was never weaker than the T-Deck.

Second, a hill. From a hillside, the same radio heard about 30 repeaters instead of one. Every message got through, and it scored 84–87% on the Bay Area health check, which counts how many of the region's listening stations hear your message. The T-Deck scored 82% from the same spot.

Same radio, same firmware, same antenna. The bug was my house.

One company makes the magic chirp. Nearly every LoRa radio runs Semtech silicon or a licensed copy. That's a supply risk, not a kill switch: the firmware is open source, and nobody can switch your radio off remotely. A movement against centralized infrastructure that depends on one chip supplier. Irony noted.

License-free isn't rule-free. ISM bands have power limits, and unlicensed users get no protection from interference. Your "I'm okay" has no more right to the airwaves than your neighbor's weather station.

Encrypted doesn't mean invisible. Public and #hashtag channels are readable by anyone, and adverts can carry your location. Leave location sharing off, especially if your bug-out cabin is a secret.

Repeaters are volunteers. Coverage depends on other people's rooftops and batteries. Treat the mesh as one layer of your comms plan: two is one, and one is none.

Reticulum isn't a mesh app but a whole cryptographic network stack that runs over LoRa, Wi-Fi, packet radio, the internet, or anything else that moves bytes. It takes config files and patience, and around the Bay I could barely find anyone on it. And no, it can't bridge MeshCore and Meshtastic; today that takes a gateway, a Raspberry Pi with one radio from each tribe.

MeshCore won't replace your phone. It's slow, text-only, and it works only because a few hundred neighbors put radios on their roofs. But that's rather the point: it's a network built by the people who use it, out of cheap radios and spare rooftops, and it keeps working when the expensive one doesn't. And when you can't get through, the answer is almost never in your settings. It's in the sky: go higher, see farther, and join the people already up there.

My T-Deck now lives in my go-bag, next to the lasagna. For the price of a takeout dinner, you can put one in yours that will, on the worst day of the year, still get the message through:

"We're fine. Bring water. And the lasagna."

#9771. 'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

Attackers could have disrupted traveler entry into Nigeria, Ethiopia, Zambia, Sri Lanka, Fiji, and Ghana via several vulnerabilities in their online visa and immigration systems.

Imagine trying to enter a country you've always wanted to visit, only to find yourself not only denied entry but potentially arrested because you've mistakenly ended up on a list of known terrorists.

This is one of several scenarios that could have unfolded if attackers had exploited flaws that independent security researcher Eaton Zveare discovered in the online passport and border-control systems of several countries: Nigeria, Ethiopia, Fiji, Zambia, Sri Lanka, and Ghana.

Though specific to each system, the flaws generally allowed unauthorized access to millions of travelers' sensitive visa and passport data — potentially including biometric information such as fingerprints — and, in some cases, even granted access to administrative functions that could be used to approve or deny entry into a country.

Specifically, Zveare discovered critical API vulnerabilities, including broken object-level authorization (BOLA), broken function-level authorization (BFLA), and missing authentication, in online systems these countries use to process visa applications and authorize travelers to enter.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Many of the systems were built by third-party contractors with varying levels of expertise, which likely contributed to the relatively simple and easily avoidable security gaps, Zveare tells Dark Reading. In Nigeria's case, an over-reliance on AI to build the systems may also have introduced flaws into the code.

"I think they've gotten on the AI hype train, and they've kind of used it to build their border control a little bit," he says.

Taken together, the vulnerabilities — which should never exist in "the systems that are vital to national security" — highlight a broader failure to secure critical national infrastructure, potentially with significant consequences for people traveling to these countries, Zveare says.

"The tip of the iceberg is not only viewing all the people who ever applied for these visas and passports, but actually being able to approve or deny applications that are currently coming in," he says, describing the potential for bad actors to exploit the flaws.

Zveare describes the level of access the flaws could provide as "God mode at the border" — also the title of a session he will lead at Black Hat Europe next month about his findings. By exploiting the vulnerabilities, attackers could effectively "have the master key to these countries and their borders," potentially threatening the safety of both citizens and people entering the country. Zveare will disclose the details of the flaws during his session, which is scheduled for Dec. 10.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

The discovery began almost by accident, when Zveare searched Microsoft Bing for the phrase "admin panel" about a year ago. One of the results led him to a private back-end portal belonging to Nigeria.

After investigating the portal, Zveare uncovered security flaws that gave him access to sensitive immigration systems. Intrigued by what he had found, he began looking for similar systems in other countries, focusing on online passport-control and visa platforms built using modern Web technologies such as Angular and React.

His search eventually led him to five more countries, where he discovered a range of vulnerabilities, including missing authentication and broken access controls — the kinds of common Web flaws that you often see but ones that "you just can't have in critical systems like this," Zveare tells Dark Reading.

In Nigeria alone, Zveare identified roughly a dozen vulnerabilities, while the other countries had several each. He went on to develop exploits to demonstrate how the flaws could allow an attacker not only to view sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to visa applicants, but also to access administrative functions that could determine whether someone was granted entry into a country.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

The potential consequences extend well beyond disrupted travel plans and compromised personal information, Zveare says. One worst-case scenario would involve an attacker identifying a high-level executive or other person of interest who might be targeted for kidnapping or assassination, then accessing their travel itinerary, hotel information, and other details that could be used to track their movements.

"You would know exactly when they land, where they are staying, and how long they're staying," Zveare says. "I'm sure you can imagine what bad people could do with that info."

Because the systems were spread across multiple foreign countries, many of which rely on outside companies to build their online infrastructure, identifying the parties responsible for fixing the vulnerabilities proved trickier than a typical bug disclosure, Zveare says.

"So all these countries have their computer emergency response teams (CERTs)," he tells Dark Reading. "Unfortunately, a lot of them did not respond."

One country whose response was particularly strong was also the one whose systems had the most problems: Nigeria, which moved quickly to resolve the vulnerabilities. Its response team had "a generally excellent response," Zveare says.

Indeed, Nigeria is emerging as "the big tech hub of Africa," and he expected its authorities to be relatively on top of these issues, he says.

When a country's CERT failed to respond, Zveare had to dig deeper to identify the independent contractor that had built the system and contact the company directly. In many cases, this proved to be the quickest route to remediation.

Overall, response times ranged from a few days to more than six months. By now, however, "everything is pretty much fixed," he says.

While Zveare says all the contractors he contacted were helpful and responsive in addressing the vulnerabilities, their security practices may have contributed to the problems in the first place.

"[The contractors] might have come in at the lowest bid, and that's what the country went with," Zveare says. "I feel as though, with how simple some of these flaws were, they might not have the most sophisticated security reviews."

One quick test Zveare uses when assessing a Web API is to look for an administrative endpoint that retrieves a list of all users. "So I'll uncover that, and I'll just copy that endpoint into my browser and see what happens."

In the case of the vulnerable border-control systems, "a lot of the time, they would just return the entire users list because they don't check for the authentication token," he says.

The problems went beyond improper token handling, however. In some cases, authentication tokens were missing altogether, meaning sensitive endpoints could be accessed without the required authentication.

This lack of fundamental Web security points to a broader failure of oversight by national authorities when selecting the contractors entrusted with building and maintaining their systems, Zveare says. For infrastructure as sensitive as border control systems, that lack of scrutiny is not only unacceptable but potentially dangerous.

"You have to properly vet these contractors because you're giving your nation's security to them," Zveare says. "And if they don't know basic Web security, you're going to have a bad time."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9770. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 13th of October 2026 07:24 PM

One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.

Why do I still own and use a computer for my business?

For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement…….

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. #9769. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9768. How to Investigate Suspected Bot Traffic in GA4

Shabnam Karbalaeihadi is a UK-based SEO strategist with nearly 10 years of experience in innovative data-driven SEO.

Shabnam Karbalaeihadi is a UK-based SEO strategist with nearly 10 years of experience in innovative data-driven SEO.

Shabnam Karbalaeihadi is a UK-based SEO strategist with nearly 10 years of experience in innovative data-driven SEO.

A spike in Direct traffic is easy to notice. The harder one to question is a spike that looks like a win. The new visitors scroll through articles, trigger plenty of events and sometimes rack up multiple page views. In a monthly performance review, that can look like audience growth.

That question matters in the age of AI search, when visits from people clicking links in AI tools and requests from automated systems can both be part of the picture. A GA4 spike can tell me where to investigate. It can’t tell me which tool generated the traffic, or whether an LLM was involved.

No single signal proves bot traffic. I look for the same sessions matching several of them, then compare reports with and without that segment.

In GA4, I start in Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition and compare the spike with a comparable period. I check which session default channel group changed, then break down the increase by landing page and country. I’m looking for where the extra sessions came from. A sitewide average can hide a surge concentrated on a single URL.

Direct means GA4 lacks a clear referral source. Unassigned means the traffic did not match a channel rule. Missing campaign tags, redirects and other attribution gaps can put legitimate visits into unexpected buckets. Google’s explanation of Direct traffic · GA4 channel definitions

For a publisher, one of my first checks is Search Console → Discover, if the report is available. If Discover clicks climb on the same articles on the same dates, that gives me a plausible explanation for at least part of the lift, especially if referral information is missing in GA4. I compare the timing and URLs because Discover clicks and GA4 sessions are different measurements. Search Console performance reports

I add Screen resolution as a breakdown in a GA4 Exploration or check the Tech details report. I pay attention when a square resolution such as 1366 × 1366 or 1600 × 1600 goes from rare to accounting for a large share of the increase. The interesting part is the concentration. How common was that resolution before the spike? Does it also dominate the same landing page, browser or country? GA4 Tech details report

If the same cluster shows substantial volume and zero or almost zero returning users over a meaningful date range, I take a closer look. Automation can start with a fresh browser profile each time, and it can also reuse one. Real visitors can look new when GA4 can’t recognise a previous visit, and a successful acquisition campaign can bring in a genuinely new audience. I compare the suspicious group with similar traffic over the same period. GA4 user metrics

On a subscription site, I check whether the extra sessions produce any verified logins or subscription activity. A SaaS team could make the same comparison with sign-ups or account activity. If a site uses a custom User type dimension, a wave of (not set) values tells me to check when the tag sends that value. It might be missing for genuine anonymous readers or because the implementation only sets it after login. I get more confidence from a mismatch between thousands of extra interactions and flat account activity, especially where comparable traffic normally produces some.

If a UK-focused publication suddenly gets a large share of its Direct sessions from Singapore or China, I check whether that lines up with distribution, coverage, or a campaign. Geography helps narrow the investigation. I’m more interested when the same sessions also share a rare resolution and repeatedly enter through one page. Country on its own is too broad a reason to exclude traffic.

Views per session below 1 is another prompt to inspect the events. GA4 counts both web page views and app screen views in this metric. If I see a low ratio, I separate web from app traffic and check whether events are arriving without their corresponding page_view or screen_view. Missing tags or an event-only implementation can explain the same pattern. I check the instrumentation before attributing it to automation. GA4 dimensions and metrics

GA4 records engagement time while a page is in focus or an app is in the foreground. An engaged session can qualify by passing the engagement-time threshold, recording a key event, or reaching two page or screen views. The default enhanced-measurement scroll event fires when 90% of the page becomes visible. Browser automation can navigate to a second page, keep a page in focus and scroll deep enough to trigger the same event. These metrics describe what the browser reported. They can look healthy even when I still have questions about who generated the activity. GA4 user engagement · Sessions · Automatically collected events

I also check unusually long engagement against the metric’s denominator. More than a day of total engagement across a large group can be ordinary. More than a day of average engagement per session is a reason to inspect event timestamps and tracking. The GA4 default of 30 minutes, adjustable up to 7 hours and 55 minutes, is an inactivity timeout. It measures how long a session can sit idle before expiring, so it doesn’t set a hard ceiling on the length of an active session. GA4 session timeout

Here’s how I set that up in a GA4 Exploration:

Where I have access, I ask the web team to compare the same URLs and time windows against CDN or server logs. Repeated request sequences or an existing bot classification can strengthen the case. Until I have that corroboration, I label the segment suspected automation. I keep the original totals visible alongside the adjusted view so stakeholders can see how much the rule changes the story.

In an illustrative example, Direct sessions fell from 9,250 to 3,820 once the segment was excluded, while all 104 verified logins and 14 subscriptions remained in the adjusted view. The outcomes didn’t move, which told me the extra sessions weren’t new readers.

Once you know which patterns deserve attention, you can use GA4 custom insights to get an email when traffic changes unexpectedly. An alert gives you a reason to investigate using the signals above.

When an alert arrives, compare the spike with campaigns and Discover performance, then examine screen resolution, returning users, geography and account outcomes. The same alert could also flag a successful article or a tracking issue. Google's guide to Analytics Insights

In a publishing report, I’d rather explain why sessions rose while verified subscriptions and returning readership stayed flat than turn that spike into an audience-growth claim. The question I bring back to the dashboard is simple.

If we take out the sessions that all behave the same way, would we still make the same decision?

Yes, for known bots. Google Analytics automatically excludes traffic from known bots and spiders, and you can’t turn this off or see how much was excluded. Automation that isn’t on a known list can still reach your reports, which is why the signals above are worth checking.

Not directly. GA4’s built-in data filters are designed for internal and developer traffic, so there is no dedicated filter for suspected bots. Instead, I build a segment around the pattern I’ve observed and compare reports with and without it.

No. Data that GA4 has already processed stays in the property, and data filters only apply going forward. For past periods, I use segments or comparisons in Explorations to show the adjusted view next to the original totals.

No. Google Discover, untagged email or app links, redirects that drop the referrer and links shared in private messages can all show up as Direct or Unassigned. I check those explanations before labelling any traffic as suspected automation.

Not reliably. GA4 can show referrals from AI tools when the referrer is passed, but it can’t tell you which tool generated automated visits. A spike shows you where to investigate. Server or CDN logs give you stronger evidence.

The SEO Metrics No One’s Tracking in the AI Era—But Should

#9767. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9766. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.
